1. Introduction
CentralandnorthAsiawasconstructedbyamalgamationofthreemainblocks,theSiberiaCraton(SIB),
the Mongolia Block (MOB; also referred to as the Amuria Block), and the North China Craton (NCC),
fromnorthtosouth(Figure1;Enkinetal.,1992).Weldingofthesethreeblockshasbeenachievedbyclo-
sureoftwomajoroceans:theMongol‐OkhotskOceanbetweentheSIBandtheMOB(VanderVooetal.,
2015;Wuetal.,2017)andthePaleo‐AsianOceanbetweentheNCCandtheMOB(Xuetal.,2013;Zhao
et al., 2013). The MOB, geographically occupying eastern and southern Mongolia, Amur region of
Russian Far East, and northeastern China, is sandwiched by the SIB to the north and the NCC to the
south, with the Mongol‐Okhotsk suture zone and the Solonker suture zone as boundaries (Xiao et al.,
2003; Zonenshain et al., 1990). Therefore, the paleoposition of the MOB in different periods is essential
tounderstand the evolution of both oceans andtiming forformationof two suture zones.The evolution
ofbothoceanshasbecomeoneofthemostcontroversialtectonicproblemsofnorthernAsiainthelastdec-
ades. For the closure timing of the Paleo‐Asian Ocean, the Late Devonian and Late Permian ages have
been proposed based on sedimentological, paleontological, geochemical, paleomagnetic, and structural
studies(Xiaoetal.,2003;Xuetal.,2013;Zhaoetal.,2013;Zhangetal.,2018).Ascissor‐stylegradualclo-
suremodelfortheMongol‐OkhotskOceanfromTriassicinthewesternsegmenttolatestJurassic‐earliest
Cretaceousintheeasternsegmenthasbeeninterpretedonthebasisofgeologicalandpaleomagneticstu-
©2020.AmericanGeophysicalUnion.
AllRightsReserved. dies(Zhaoetal.,1990;Zorin,1999;Kravchinsky,Sorokin,&Courtillot,2002,Kravchinsky,Cogné,etal.,
ZHAOETAL. 1of16

### page_3
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2019JB017338
2002; Metelkin et al., 2010). However, west‐east simultaneous closure of the Mongol‐Okhotsk Ocean
during the latest Jurassic‐earliest Cretaceous has also been proposed based on a compilation of
paleomagneticdata(VanderVooetal.,2015).
Inthelastfewdecades,severalpaleomagneticstudieshavebeencarriedoutinMongolia.However,dueto
the insufficient paleomagnetic data and contradicting conclusions deduced from these data, the Late
PaleozoicpaleopositionoftheMOBanditsrelationshiptotheSIBandtheNCCarestillhighlydebatable.
Pruner(1987,1992)performedthefirstpaleomagneticstudyontheCarboniferousandPermianstratain
northernandcentralMongolia,andthe datashowedalow(~20°N)paleolatitudeforthe MOB,whichis
consistent with that of the NCC. Therefore, the author suggested that central and northern Mongolia
had probably been a part of the NCC during Permian, and far away (~40° distance) from the SIB
(Pruner, 1987, 1992). Kovalenko and Chernov (2008) reported an Early Permian pole from the Daribi
Ridge in western Mongolia. However, this pole is calculated from number of samples rather than sites
and therefore no fold test can be applied. Moreover, the data show very high paleolatitudes (45–60°N),
which enabled the authors to suggest that western Mongolia was located at the southern margin of the
SIB and separated from the NCC by an ocean with width of ~2,000 km (Kovalenko & Chernov, 2008).
As the samples were collected from the southern part of the Tuva‐Mongolia microblock that accreted to
the SIB during the Neoproterozoic‐Early Paleozoic, this pole may not be able to represent the MOB.
Edel et al. (2014) reported paleomagnetic data from Carboniferous volcanic rocks and granodiorites in
southwesternMongolia.However,asnofoldtestwasapplied,thecomponentsisolatedareeitherremag-
netizedorhaveanunclearageofremanenceacquisition.
Therefore,uptonow,reliableLatePaleozoicpaleomagneticpolesarestillrarefortheMOB.Paleomagnetic
resultsfromwell‐datedstrataareneededtoconstrainthepaleogeographicevolutionoftheMOBintheLate
PaleozoicandtofurtherunderstandtheevolutionofboththePaleo‐AsianOceanandtheMongol‐Okhotsk
Ocean.Inordertoachievethesegoals,wecarriedoutpaleomagneticstudiesontheEarlyPermianvolcanic
stratainnortheasternMongolia.
2. Geological Background andSampling
In northeastern Mongolia, the core MOB is constituted by the Precambrian Ereendavaa Terrane, which
extends eastward into northeastern China and Russian Far East (Figure 1; Badarch et al., 2002).
RadiometricagedataarerareforthisterraneintheMongolianpart.However,intheRussianpart,zircon
U‐Pbdatingofabiotitegranitesamplegaveanageof740±20Ma(Bibikovaetal.,1979).Inaddition,gran-
itoidsandgabbroswithagesof851±6Mato737±5MahavebeenidentifiedalongtheArgunRiverin
northeasternChina(Tangetal.,2013).ThePrecambrianbasementisoverlainbyNeoproterozoicmetasedi-
mentary and metavolcanic rocks and intruded by granitoids with Cambrian to Devonian ages (Badarch
etal.,2002).Ordovician‐Siluriansandstoneandlimestonehavebeenwidelyidentifiedalongitssouthern
margin. All the pre‐Permian rocks are intruded by Permian‐Triassic granitoids (Badarch et al., 2002). In
itsnorthernpart,aPermianvolcanicsequenceandaTriassic‐Jurassicsedimentarysequencewereidentified
(Donskayaetal.,2013).Triassic‐Jurassicstrataalongitsnorthernmarginexperiencedsevereductiledefor-
mationduetotheMongol‐Okhotskorogeny.
TheEarlyPermianGazarFormationiswellexposedintheBayandunregiontothesouthoftheMongol‐
Okhotsk suture (Figures 1 and 2). This volcanic‐dominated sequence is mainly composed of rhyolite,
dacite, andesite, and tuff, with subordinate siltstone and sandstone interlayers. Due to posterior tectonic
events,thisformationshowshighlytiltedorevenverticalbeddingswithtightfolds(Table1).Theageof
this volcanic sequence has been assigned to the Early Permian during previous geological mapping.
However, there are no fossil or radiometric data; thus, the age of this formation is not well constrained.
Therefore, we collected one rhyolite sample for zircon U‐Pb dating to determine the age of this volcanic
sequence,whichwillalsocontributetoourpaleomagneticanalysisandforcomparisonwithcoevalpaleo-
magneticpolesfromnearbyblocks.
Overall, 69 cores of nine sites were drilled from the Early Permian Gazar Formation in northwestern
Bayandun(Figure2andTable1).Sites08‐13weresampledfromsectionA,andsites14–16werecollected
from section B (1.5 km to the northeast of section A). Sections A and B represent two limbs of a fold

3. Analytical Procedures
3.1. ZirconU‐PbDating
Zircongrainswereinitiallyselectedbyheavyliquidseparationandthenpurifiedwithamagneticsepara-
tiontechnique.Thegrainsleftwerethenhandpickedunderabinocularmicroscope.Pickedzirconswere
embeddedinanepoxyresinandhalf‐sectioned.Allgrainsmountedwerephotographedunderanoptical
microscope with both reflected and transmitted light to reveal surface flaws and internal inclusions.
Finally,theyweresubjectedtocathodoluminescence(CL)torevealinternaltexturesenablingustochoose
target spots for further U‐Pb dating. The CL imaging was carried out with a Quanta 200 FEG Scanning
Electron Microscope in the SEEL lab of Peking University. Zircon U‐Pb analysis was performed at the
Key Laboratory of Orogeny and Crust Evolution (Peking University) using a LA‐ICP‐MS system with a
193‐nmArFExcimerlaserandanAgilient7500cICP‐MS.NIST610andSiwereusedasexternalandinter-
nalstandardstocalibratezirconanalyses.ZirconstandardsPlesovice(337Ma)and91500wereusedtocor-
rect U‐Pb isotope fractionation effects and to monitor the age measurement deviation, respectively.
Calculation of element concentrations and isotopic ratios was done with the GLITTER software (ver.
4.4.2) designed by Macquarie University. For common lead correction, we follow Andersen's (2002)
method.ConcordiaageswerecalculatedbyIsoplot/Excel(3.0),withtheweightedmeanagesat95%con-
fidencelevel(Ludwig,2003).
3.2. Paleomagnetism
Coreswerecutinto2.2‐cm‐longstandardspecimensinthelaboratory.Beforemagneticremanencemeasure-
ments,severalinvestigationswereperformedtodeterminemagneticcarriers:high‐temperaturethermomag-
netic runs of magnetic susceptibility (κ‐T) using a CS3 furnace‐coupled KLY‐3S kappabridge, acquisition

Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2019JB017338
Figure2.GeologicalmapoftheBayandunregionshowingthepaleomagneticsamplinglocation(fromMineralResources
AuthorityofMongolia&MongolianAcademyofScience,1998).
curveofisothermalremanentmagnetization(IRM)byimpartingIRMswithaMMPM9pulsemagnetizerand
measuring IRM intensities with a Minispin spinner magnetometer, and magnetic hysteresis curve
measurements using a Princeton Measurements MicroMag 2900 Alternating Gradient Magnetometer
(AGM). All these rock magnetic analyses were done in the magnetic laboratory of University
Tübingen,Germany.
Foreachsite,sixtoeightspecimenswerechosenfordemagnetization.Magneticremanencewasprogres-
sivelyremovedin13to16stepsusingboththermalandalternatingmagneticfield(AF)techniques.Thetem-
peratureintervalsarefrom20to100°C,andthealternatingmagneticfieldintervalsarefrom2to20mT.For
thermaltreatment,amodelTD‐48SCthermaldemagnetizer(ASCScientificCompany)wasused.Magnetic
remanences were measured with a 2G Enterprises u‐channel DC‐SQUID (Model 755–1.65 UC) magnet-
ometer.Adegausserisimplementedinthemagnetometersystemforalternatingfielddemagnetization.
Magneticdirectionswerecalculatedusingprincipalcomponentanalysismethod(Kirschvink,1980).Fisher
spherical analysis was used to compute mean magnetic directions. Individual direction isolation, mean
direction computation, and pole calculation and comparison were achieved by the softwares Paleomag
(Cogné,2003),PMGSC(designedbyR.Enkin),andRemasoft(designedbyAGICO).

5. Discussion
5.1. ComparisonofPermianPaleomagneticPoles
Paleosecularvariation(PSV)isafundamentalproblemforpaleomagneticdatafromvolcanicrocks,asto
whetherthePSVhasbeenaveragedoutornot,andwillinfluencethereliabilityofthedataset.Therefore,
beforecomparisonofpaleomagneticpoles,wefirstexaminedthePSVproblemofourdataset.Inorderto
averageoutsecularvariation,wesampledfromtwosections.Forthedataset,theFisherprecisionparameter
k values of site‐mean directions are mostly in the range of 20–63 (Table 1), indicating relative scatter of
paleomagnetic directions for individual specimen within each site. Moreover, the A value (5.7°) of the
95
VGPislowerthantheA value(7.8°)calculatedafterDeenenetal.(2011),indicatingthatPSVmayhave
95min
alreadybeenaveragedoutwithineachsite.However,theangulardispersionS(=8.7)oftheVGPsofthe
seven sites is slightly lower than that of expected PSV from the TK03.GAD model at the same latitude
(Tauxe&Kent,2004),indicatingthatthePSVisnotfullyaveragedout.Eventhoughourdatamightnot
be adequate to fully average out secular variation, they support previous paleolatitude estimate of the
MOB without the problem of secular variation. Therefore, we can still use this pole for comparison and
tectonicdiscussion.

LatePaleozoic,especiallyPermian,strataarewidelydistributedinnortheasternMongolia,whichprovidea
good opportunity for paleomagnetic study. Pruner (1987, 1992) reported an Early Permian and a Late
PermianpaleomagneticpolefromnorthernandcentralMongolia,butnofoldtestcouldbeappliedforeither
ofthese(Table2andFigure7).AlthoughbothnormalandreversepolaritieshavebeenfoundintheEarly
Permianstrata,specimenswithnormalpolarityaccountfor74%ofthetotalspecimens(Pruner,1992),which
is inconsistent with the PCRS. Therefore, this Early Permian pole might be questionable. Pruner's data
(1987,1992)showalowpaleolatitude(11–21°N)forMongoliaduringthePermian.Ourdataprovidethefirst
EarlyPermianpaleomagneticpolefromNEMongolia,whichalsoindicatesalowpaleolatitude(~18.3°N)for
Mongolia. Three Permian poles were reported from the Chita area of Russia (Figure 7; Xu et al., 1997;
Kravchinsky,Cogné,etal.,2002),whichisconsideredasthenorthernmarginoftheMOB.Thesethreepoles
alsocorrespondtoalow(~20°N)paleolatitudesimilartothedataobtainedfromMongolia(Figure8).
For the southernpart ofthe MOB, five paleomagneticpoles havebeen reportedfromInner Mongolia in
northernChina(Table2;X.Zhaoetal.,1990;Chenetal.,1997;Lietal.,2012;P.Zhaoetal.,2013;Zhangetal.,
2018).PolesobtainedbyChenetal.(1997)andLietal.(2012)arebothfromtheBaoligaomiaoFormationin
northern Inner Mongolia. The similar bedding attitude makes fold tests impossible for either of them.
AlthoughbothnormalandreversepolaritieshavebeenisolatedbyChenetal.(1997),thenormalandreverse

causedbylateMesozoicoverprintthathasnotbeencompletelycleaned(Chenetal.,1997).Therefore,this
polemightbequestionableandwewillnotuseitforfurtherdiscussion.SamplesfromLietal.(2012)show
unifiedreversepolarities,whichareconsistentwiththePCRS.ThepolecalculatedbyLietal.(2012)isclose
tothePermianpoleofInnerMongolia(Zhaoetal.,1990).Therefore,wemaytentativelyconsiderthattheC ‐

5.2. TectonicImplications
5.2.1. ClosureofthePaleo‐AsianOcean
TimingfortheMOB‐NCCcollisionisessentialfortheevolutionofthesoutheasternsegmentofPaleo‐Asian
Ocean.FromcomparisonofDevonianpolesoftheMOBandtheNCC,Kravchinsky,Sorokin,andCourtillot
(2002)foundnegligiblepaleolatitudedifferencebetweenthetwoblocks,indicatingthattheMOBwasvery
closetotheNCCinthistimeperiod.Besides,mostpreviouspaleomagneticresultssupportsimilarpaleola-
titudesfortheMOBandtheNCCduringtheEarlyPermian(Figure8;Pruner,1992;Chenetal.,1997;Li
etal.,2012;Zhaoetal.,2013),whichleadstheseauthorstoproposeaweldedMOB‐NCCatleastsincethe
EarlyPermian.However,recentpaleomagneticresultssuggestedthatpreviousdatafromtheMOBthatwere
mainly obtained from clastic rocks might be affected by inclination shallowing (Zhang et al., 2018). By
adjustment of the inclination shallowing with an optimal flattening factor of f = 0.6, Zhang etal. (2018)
placed the MOB at a relatively high paleolatitude of 30.8–32.0°N from Late Carboniferous to Late
PermianandproposedthattheMOBwasstillseparatedfromtheNCCbythePaleo‐AsianOceanduring
the Early Permian. However, with the same flattening factor, the Permian paleolatitude of the NCC
increasedfrom21.5°Nto30.2°N(Zhangetal.,2018),similarasthatoftheMOB.Thismeansthatinclination
shallowingofpaleomagneticdatadoesnotaffecttherelativepositionoftheNCCandMOB,andtheNCC

5.2.2. EarlyStageoftheMongol‐OkhotskOcean
Most research works of the Mongol‐Okhotsk Ocean are focused on the closure of different segments of
this3,000‐km‐longorogenicbelt,whereastheearlystageevolutionofthisbeltispoorlyunderstood.The
western part of the Mongol‐Okhotsk Belt recorded its early stage evolution, where Devonian and
Carboniferous clastic turbidite deposits are widely distributed (Zonenshain et al., 1990). Meanwhile,
two ophiolitic mélanges with zircon U‐Pb ages of 325–314 Ma have been reported from the Adaatsag
and Khuhu Davaa regions in central Mongolia, representing remnants of the Mongol‐Okhotsk oceanic
crust (Tomurtogoo et al., 2005; Zhu et al., 2018). By reviewing geological and geochemical studies on
the Late Paleozoic‐Mesozoic magmatic rocks on the northern side of the Mongol‐Okhotsk suture zone,
Donskaya et al. (2013) suggested that the northward Mongol‐Okhotsk oceanic subduction began in the
Devonian and reached its climax in the Permian‐Triassic. The subduction was revealed by the middle
Carboniferous‐Triassic Selenge Arc (Donskaya et al., 2013). On the southern side of this belt, Zhao,
Xu,andJahn(2017)reportedthreePermian(273–254 Ma)subduction‐relatedgraniticmassifsineastern
Mongolia. By compilation of published age data of Permian and Triassic magmatic rocks from north-
easternMongolia andnortheasternChina, Zhao, Xu, andJahn(2017) proposeda Permian‐Triassic mag-
matic pulse along the north margin of the MOB. Therefore, subduction of the Mongol‐Okhotsk oceanic
crust beneath both the southern SIB (present coordinate) and the northern MOB is indicated during
Permian‐Triassic (Figure 9).
ForthePermo‐Carboniferousperiod,paleomagneticstudiesontheSIBmainlyfocusedonthelatestPermian
(ca.251Ma)Siberianbasaltictrap(Table2).ConsistentLatePermianpoleshavebeenobtainedfromdifferent
parts of the SIB (Table 2 and Figure 7). Unlike the large data set of Late Permian poles, only one Early
Permian(275±4Ma)paleomagneticpolewasobtainedfrommaficdykesatthesouthernmarginofthe
SIBneartheBaikalLake(Pisarevskyetal.,2006).Solereversepolaritythatisconsistentwiththe PCRS,
andapositivebakedcontacttestwasusedtoargueforaprimaryremanence(Pisarevskyetal.,2006).This
Early Permian pole indicates a high paleolatitude at ~79°N for the SIB during the Early Permian
(Figure8).However,thishighpaleolatitudeisconflictingwiththeEarlyPermianpaleogeographicrecon-
structionoftheSIBbasedonitsAPWP,inwhichtheSIBislocatedatapaleolatitudeof40°–65°(Figure8;
e.g.,Smethurstetal.,1998;Cocks&Torsvik,2007;Metelkinetal.,2012).ThisdifferenceleadsPisarevsky
etal.(2006)toproposethattheSIBwasnotconnectedwithLaurasiaby275Ma.Thediscussionofthisdiffer-
enceisbeyondthescopeofthispaper.HereweusetheEarlyPermianpolefromtheAPWPoftheSIBfor
paleogeographicreconstruction(Figure9).ConsideringthelowpaleolatitudeoftheMOB(~12°–24°),there
wasalarge(~30°)latitudinaldifferencebetweentheMOBandtheSIBduringtheEarlyPermian,andthis
latitudinal difference increased in Late Permian due to the northward migration of the SIB (Figure 8;
Smethurst et al., 1998; Cocks & Torsvik, 2007). This latitudinal difference can be interpreted by the
Mongol‐OkhotskOceanbetweentheSIBandtheMOB(Figure9).
NotethattheKazakhstanBlockhadjoinedLaurussiabytheUralianOrogenyduringtheLateCarboniferous
to earliest Permian (Cocks & Torsvik, 2007), and the SIB welded with the Kazakhstan Block in the Late
Carboniferous‐Early Permian, forming the proto‐Eurasia continent (Abrajevitch et al., 2008; Filippova
et al., 2001). Paleomagnetic data show that the southern margin of the proto‐Eurasia continent (present
shapeandposition)waslongitude‐parallelduringthePermian(Figure9;Kravchinsky,Cogné,etal.,2002;
VanderVooetal.,2015).Incontrast,thenorthernmarginoftheMOBfacedtothenortheast (Figure9;
Zhaoetal.,2013).Inthiscase,thereisa>100°intersectionanglebetweenthewesternandsouthernmargins
oftheMongol‐OkhotskOcean(Figure9).Thiskindofpaleogeographicpatternresultedintheproposalthat
subduction along the two continental margins might belong to one subduction belt (e.g., Zorin, 1999).
Meanwhile,geologicalstudiessuggestthattheTarimCratonhascollidedwiththeKazakhstanBlockduring
theLateCarboniferous(e.g.,B.Hanetal.,2011),buttheconnectionbetweentheTarimCratonandtheNCC‐
MOBduringtheEarlyPermianisstillunclear(Figure9).Althoughthisproblemisoutofscopeofthisstudy,
itrelatestoanimportantissueofwhethertheMongol‐OkhotskOceanwasconnectedwiththePaleo‐Tethys
ZHAOETAL. 13of16

### page_15
Journal of Geophysical Research: Solid Earth 10.1029/2019JB017338
OceanduringPermian(Enkinetal.,1992;Gilderetal.,2008;VanderVooetal.,2015;Wuetal.,2017).More
geologicalandpaleomagneticstudiesareneededtouncoverthisproblem.
5.2.3. IntracontinentalStrikeSlip
AllpaleomagneticpolesobtainedfromtheMOBdistributedalongasmallcircle(Figure7),indicatingthat
theunifiedNCC‐MOBisnotarigidblock,whichcanbeascribedtoposteriorintracontinentalvertical‐axis
strike‐slip‐relatedrotations,especiallyalongprevioussuturezones(e.g.,Zhaoetal.,2015).Thestrike‐slip‐
relatedrotationshavebeenreportedbypreviouspaleomagneticandstructuralstudies(Enkinetal.,1992;
Metelkinetal.,2010;Zhaoetal.,2015),representedbyMesozoicshearzoneswithinandalongthemargin
oftheMOB(e.g.,XilamulunFaultZoneandEastGobiFaultZone;Webbetal.,2010;Zhaoetal.,2015).Itis
notedthatpaleomagneticpolesoftheMOBfromInnerMongoliapartoverlapwithpolesfromtheNCC,
indicatingthatnosignificantrotationoccurredforthispartsincePermian.However,polesoftheMOBfrom
theMongoliapartshowdifferentdegreesofanticlockwiserotationrelativetopolesoftheNCC(Figure7),
whichmaybeinducedbythesinistralshearalongtheEastGobiFaultZone(Webbetal.,2010).Onthecon-
trary,polesoftheMOBfromtheAmurregioninRussiashowalargedegreeofclockwiserotationsrelativeto
polesoftheNCC(Figure7),whichmightbeascribedtothefactthatsamplelocationsforthesethreepoles
are all located inside of the Mongol‐Okhotsk suture zone. Post‐Jurassic strike‐slip movement along this
suture zone may cause significant internal rotations. Detailed studies on the East Gobi Fault Zone and
XilamulunFaultZonehavebeenperformed,whichshowsLateTriassicstrike‐slipmovementsofthesefaults
that weretriggered byfar‐fieldstresseffectdueto theTriassic collisionbetween theNCC andthe South
ChinaCraton(e.g.,Zhaoetal.,2015),andcoevalclosureofthewesternpartoftheMongol‐OkhotskOcean
(e.g.,Metelkinetal.,2010;Zhaoetal.,2015).
6. Conclusions
InordertouncovertheLatePaleozoicpaleogeographicpositionoftheMOBandfurtherunderstandevolu-
tionofboththePaleo‐AsianOceanandtheMongol‐OkhotskOcean,apaleomagneticstudyisperformedon
the EarlyPermianvolcanic stratain theBayandun regionof northeasternMongolia.ZirconU‐Pb dating
resultsrevealanEarlyPermianage(283±3Ma)forthestudiedvolcanicstrata.Magneticmineralogyinves-
tigationsrevealmagnetiteandTi‐magnetiteasthemainmagneticcarriers.Magneticdirectionalisolation
displaysbothprimaryandsecondarymagnetizations.ChRMdirectionsisolatedfromsevensitesshowcon-
sistent reverse polarity, corresponding to the Permo‐Carboniferous (Kiaman) Reverse Superchron. Site‐
mean directions pass fold tests, and an Early Permian paleomagnetic pole is calculated for the MOB at
λ/φ=−14.9°N/76.8°E(A =5.7°)withN=7sites.AllpublishedPermianpaleomagneticpolesfromthe
95
MOBarealignedalongasmallcirclewiththesamplinglocationascenter,andthissmallcircleintersects
PermianpolesfromtheNCCbutfarawayfromthosefromtheSIB.Thesecharacteristicsindicatethat(1)
theMOBshouldhaveweldedwiththeNCC beforethe EarlyPermianorwasatleastclosetoit.(2)The
weldedMOB‐NCCwasseparatedfromtheSIBbytheMongol‐OkhotskOceanwith~30°latitudinaldiffer-
enceintheEarlyPermian.(3)Significantvertical‐axisstrike‐slip‐relatedrotationsoccurredwithinandalong
themarginsoftheunifiedMOB‐NCCduetofar‐fieldstresseffectproducedbyposteriororogenicevents.
